utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I think we are at the point where we could continue the examination-in-chief of the witness Sokolar. I see that the usher is already trying to find him. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. In relation to this witness, it happened that the Defence had to spend the better part of the night in order to solve the problem, to look at the look at the invoices, and it looks as if I'm going to have to ask several more questions after Ms. Pilipovic, if the Chamber will let me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sokolar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps unnecessary, but may I remind you of the solemn declaration you made yesterday at the beginning of your continual -- testimony yesterday. Yes, then you may continue your examination-in-chief. Please proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Sokolar, when we broke yesterday, you were describing how the city had become divided on the basis of ethnicity of the residents. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber which neighbourhoods became predominantly Serb once the war started?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were predominantly the settlements where there was a majority Serb population, and I told you yesterday that this was Rajlovac, Nedzarici, Lukavica, and then later on it was also the case of Ilidza, Vogosca, Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Once the war started, how did your police duties change?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Considering that there was real chaos as far as property of the state was concerned, cars, shops, there were many crimes that were committed, and we tried as much as we could to identify the perpetrators. And occasionally I also started to have duties that I hadn't had so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did there come a time shortly after the war broke out that you became aware of sniping activities?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Considering that this was by the municipality Novi Grad and I lived in Dobrinja, there was a need to have someone from the crime department work in did Dobrinja, and I was aware that there was sniping activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How did you become aware of this sniping activity?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were areas it was impossible to go to. At first, these were just intersections, and then later on there were physical obstacles, roadblocks, for instance, containers, all the damaged cars, lorries, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When did those roadblocks and barricades begin being established?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: These roadblocks started to be put up as checkpoints, when there were people present as well. And these were physical obstacles, as I mentioned, and this was the period early April. And in fact it was April and it went on until about mid-May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, the year was 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And at that point in time, May of 1992, where were you officially posted as a police officer?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In May 1992, I still was supposed to be in the centre of the Novi Grad municipality, but this was near the Alipasino settlement in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did there come a time shortly thereafter that your duty station changed?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I lived in Dobrinja, for a period of time, because of sniping activity, it was impossible to get from Dobrinja to the Olympic Village and to the military field near Dobrinja V. And so Dobrinja was cut off from the city and I was unable to get to work for a whole week.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you then begin working out of a police office in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the phone, I spoke to my superiors, and I went to the centre, about the 10th of May that was, and I was later told that I should work in Dobrinja where I would set up and where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you establish a small police station in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to stress that because of the events in Slovenia and Croatia, there was a plan --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hear the interpretation booth, and they are asking the witness to approach the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please come a bit closer to the microphone. Thank you for your assistance, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Sokolar, I would like to focus your attention on establishing the police station in Dobrinja. Did there come a time when you did that?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to explain that because of the events in Croatia and in Slovenia, at the end of 1991, just before 1992, what was created was a reserve police force. And this force was the same in structure as the active force, there were all three ethnic -- ethnicities represented. And in April, when there was a departure, and when there were two or even, in some cases, three MUPs or CSBs, and after the workers of Serbian origin left, then in areas this was also the same case. And in Dobrinja, there was a unit of police established as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did this include both reserve and active-duty police?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did. As I said, this was November/December 1991. There was already a part of the reserve force, and I said that the workers of Serb origin, although they were active, they left, they departed, and they created and established other new stations, public security stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So from approximately mid-1992 onwards, you were posted out of the police office in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly from June 1992, I was in Dobrinja. I lived in Dobrinja, and I worked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And did you remain working and living in Dobrinja throughout the duration of the war?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, until the end of the war, I lived and worked in Dobrinja. Only occasionally I went out into the city, but very rarely. If there was a need to do that, I would go to the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And during the course of the war, as you were posted in Dobrinja, did a large part of your responsibilities include investigating sniping incidents?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to clarify that because Dobrinja was surrounded for quite a long time, so it was impossible -- we were cut off. It was impossible to communicate because there were also periods without electricity, without telephone connection. It wasn't possible to use a telephone or the fax. So I was forced to do jobs that I hadn't done until then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please provide some examples of these types of jobs.

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was -- this was going to the local hospital. This was first a surgery infirmary, and then it became a local hospital. So what would happen is that the practice was that they would call us and inform us there were wounded people or those who were killed so we would go to the hospital. We would check the identity of the person in question, the type of injury, and then later on, if it was possible, we would go to the scene of the incident if the situation allowed it, of course, or at least the vicinity of the location where the incident happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: These people who you've indicated were taken to the hospital with wounds, what type of wounds did these people sustain?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many different kinds of injuries from shelling, and there were also from bullets, from automatic bullets. There were exit and entry wounds. And of course when shells were in question, then of course there were also amputations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the last six months of 1992, approximately how many times were you summoned to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to stress that a number of casualties, people who died as well as those who were wounded in the course of 1992 were not really recorded, registered. Perhaps there are data in the local hospital in Dobrinja. But we -- myself, I speak for myself, I did not get any instruction as to record these incidents. It's only really in 1993 that we started to work seriously on identification and recording of these sniping activities and shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During 1993, if you recall, approximately how many times or how frequently would you be summoned to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were days where it could happen that I would go three or four times a day, and then there were days with no activity. So it happened that it could be either three or four days during the day or sometimes days with no activity at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know approximately how many sniping incidents you investigated during 1993 in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to stress again that I did not go myself to these investigations. If it was possible, if the situation allowed it, I was given assistance from the centre of the town, from the city, if it was possible to have a proper team established with the investigating judge and other experts who would assist me in the investigation, particularly in the cases where there were more than one person killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did the situation with respect to sniping continue during 1994?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did. Sniping activity continued in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During 1994, were you also summoned to the hospital to investigate persons injured due to sniping?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was the usual practice. Whenever someone would be injured, taken to a hospital, the personnel, either the doctor or the nurses, would inform us that there were wounded people, and we would then go and take their personal details. And as I said, if it was possible, we would go to the scene of the incident or the vicinity of the scene of the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know approximately how frequently you went to the hospital during 1994?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't really say. Quite a lot of time has passed since then, six years ago. So I couldn't tell you the exact number, but there were several cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Sokolar, you testified a few moments ago that Dobrinja was surrounded. Do you know if there were parts of Dobrinja that were held by the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were two areas of Dobrinja that were under their control. This was Dobrinja IV and part of Dobrinja I. And also, the settlement around the airport, it could be considered that it was under their control.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: As part of your crime prevention duties during 1993 and 1994, did that include a public awareness of sniping incidents?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't my duty exactly. The policemen were in charge of that who were patrolling the streets and who were informing the citizens and telling about the places, locations where it was dangerous to cross the streets or to be in an open area, unprotected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: As a result of the investigations that you conducted into sniping in Dobrinja in 1993 and 1994, did you reach any conclusions as to the locations where the snipers were situated at the time these incidents occurred?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Considering the configuration of the terrain, looking from Dobrinja, this came from Dobrinja IV, Dobrinja I, from the village of Nedzarici, and also the settlement around the airport. So it came from these locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you ever conduct an investigation where you reached the conclusion that perhaps the school of theology was a source of sniping fire?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I cannot remember how many cases, but I believe I did. Yes, I would like to also stress that every time I went out to the scene of the incidents, it was recorded. I would make an official note, short note, and I would inform my superiors about these incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask the witness be shown a document marked P3267.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Excuse me, do you mean 2367?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Indeed I do. Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Sokolar, I would like you to take a look at the document that you have just been handed and tell the Trial Chamber what this document is.

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can see here is a document which contains the description of the incident including my official note, including medical documentation. So as much as I can see, I think I can remember what it was all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Is this document one of the reports that you would have produced following the reporting of a sniping incident?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is an official note that I wrote about going to the hospital, and going to the vicinity of the scene of the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the specifics of this incident?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I can. In fact, I can see that this is about shooting at the bus which was carrying passengers and arriving in Dobrinja. It stopped in the centre, and while the bus was standing, it was hit near a tyre, and two ladies were injured. I first went to the hospital where I spoke to the personnel, and I found out about their injuries. The bus -- the bus had gone, gone to the garage, and there it is -- my colleagues went to the garage and looked at the bus. So it was established that it was hit from the right-hand side -- on the right-hand side near the tyre while it was standing. And I believe that these are exit and entry wounds Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of the two ladies. I think in one lady's case it was one leg, and in the second lady's case, it was both legs. Let me just have a look at it. Yes. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Sokolar, do you recall the approximate location in Dobrinja where this bus was located at the time it was fired upon?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Considering that I have been living in Dobrinja now for 20 years, and I know Dobrinja rather well, the bus had stopped in a wide intersection, large street between the buildings of streets in Nikole Demonje Street and Omladinskih Radnih Brigada Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And did your investigation lead you to any conclusions as to the source of fire in this incident?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bus was standing in front of or just before the intersection, after arriving in Dobrinja, and there was a grassy area. Now there is a small shopping centre. It's no longer an open area. This is where it had stopped. And it was open. It was then -- the fire was opened on the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you reach any conclusions about where the sniper was located who shot at the bus?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Considering that the bus was standing when we arrived in the vicinity of the scene of the incident, and looking at the direction where the bullet could have come from, I think it could -- we could conclude that this came from up above Dobrinja, so from the direction of Nedzarici. That means between two blocks -- two apartment blocks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask that the witness be shown the map which is marked P3097.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Sokolar, do you recall meeting with an investigator from the International Tribunal in 1995?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They came on several occasions, and they called me for an interview. And I believe that we also went to the scene of the incident. I can't quite remember. We went to several scenes of the incident where there was also -- there had also been shelling, also sniping. So I can't quite remember whether it was them that I went with because we went to all of these scenes and also the areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the course of the interview in 1995, do you remember being handed a map and being asked to make certain markings on the map?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. I was shown a map of Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd ask you to take a look at the map to your right and tell the Trial Chamber if that is the map that you, in fact, marked during the course of an interview in 1995.

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the map. I can even recognise my handwriting. I used a red ballpoint to write the demarcation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please indicate on the map where you made that demarcation line.

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, this is the line, towards Dobrinja I and Dobrinja IV localities, and it is not indicated on the way towards Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Next to the demarcation line that you drew on this map, did you also place some words in the Bosnian language next to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it be possible, perhaps, to put the north upwards and this is easier for our orientation, and perhaps then zoom in a bit more on Dobrinja, and put that in the centre. Yes -- perhaps, put up the map a tiny little bit up, Mr. Usher, could you please. Yes, I think that's ... Please proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Sokolar, next to the demarcation line which you indicated on the map, did you also write some words --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Could you please point out again the demarcation line, please.

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The demarcation line on one side was between Dobrinja I and -- went between Dobrinja I and Dobrinja IV, and this is where I drew it by hand. And I then wrote there the demarcation line. And there are some other markings, green ones, but these are only pointers, indications, for the Nedzarici locality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, with respect to the demarcation line that you made on the right-hand side of the map, did you mark that with two words in the Bosnian language?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only see what I wrote here, and that is the demarcation line. Linja Razjanicena (phoen), that is the only thing. I also put 1, 2, 3. Oh, I see here number 7, 6, but no other characters. And I also wrote up in the corner, the 8th of November, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Can you please describe for us by number what the various markings that you made on this map indicate, starting with number 1. And if you can also point to them as you're describing what those markings indicate, please.

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 1, I think this is Dobrinja I locality, and Miroslava Krleze Street. The arrow is pointing at -- I believe it's called Janka Julovica Street. I think it is Janka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know what the circle next to the number 2 represents?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this here is an open area between Dobrinja I and Dobrinja IV, and there was - and still is - a church which was under construction then, an orthodox church.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did any of your investigations into sniping incidents lead you to conclude that that church was the source of sniper fire?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. On the bridge, there were a number of incidents. I don't know how documented that is. But that's quite true, there were some activities on the bridge; that is, inside the locality of Dobrinja as you go from Dobrinja II to Dobrinja III.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: This bridge that you've mentioned, Mr. Sokolar, does this arrow pointing next to the number 2, upwards and to the left, indicate the location of that bridge?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arrow number 2 points -- yes, indicates the bridge between these two localities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you investigate sniping incidents involving persons who were shot while they were crossing that bridge?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how many such incidents involved persons in the immediate vicinity of that bridge?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a number of incidents, both on the bridge and in the open area between the streets Grada Bakua and other buildings. There were some activities there on the corner of Grada Bakua Street. I'm sorry I'm using the old names of the streets. Now they have all been changed but I don't know what they are called.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Sokolar, is there a circle with a number 3 in it anywhere on this map?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Down here, on the left-hand side of the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what is the building next to the number 3 indicate?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This here, all the way downstream, a small river, I believe this is the faculty of theology, and near the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Sokolar, can you indicate to us or please tell us what the circle with the number 4 indicates on this map.

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's something -- oh, here, number 4. I see. Number 4, this could be the Aerodrom locality, that is, the buildings in the locality, Aerodrom, airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Is that the area that you referred to earlier as the airport settlement?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. It is in the immediate vicinity of the airport, and that is where its called Aerodrom, airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did your investigations lead you to conclude that the area near the number 4 was also the source of sniper fire?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from Aerodrom next to Danko Mitrov's building, and these are small numbers, to the end of the building here. There was a parking lot here, and from that direction, one could also, more or less, target the area of our out-patient clinic, that is, hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Sokolar, what does the area marked by the number 5 in a circle represent?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five, I've just been explaining. This is a parking lot, and there is some greenery between those buildings. And that is why, from the Aerodrom locality, snipers could aim at this. And between the buildings on Omladinskih, Radnih Brigada, near the hospital. That is number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what number 6, which is immediately above the 5, can you tell us what the number 6 indicates?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This here is illegible, but number 6 is at the exit from Dobrinja. This here is illegible. I would say that this is 5, but this here. Number 6, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes. That is the exit from Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Exit from Dobrinja, exit from Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you see a circle with the number 7 in it anywhere on the map?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is in Dobrinja III.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you see --

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: But, there's two places in Dobrinja III -- no. Dobrinja I, I see Dobrinja III, I see number 7 in three different places here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know what those number 7s indicate?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 7s are squares in the centre, residential blocks, which also had atomic shelters. That's what we call them. These are underground areas where ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: These were underground Civil Protection, Civil Defence shelters?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was their purpose, even though like before the war, some of them were used as business outlets, small shops or something like that. They were never used for their -- for what they had been originally intended, only very little and at the beginning. But later on it was destroyed and there were no lights or anything, so I do not think they served a purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Sokolar, the investigations that you conducted into sniping, did those investigations concern civilian victims or military victims or both?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to mention, because I worked in the police, I did not conduct an investigation outside in the area or along the demarcation line where we would have military conscripts, rather, members of the BH army. All the investigations I performed were in different settlements where one had civilians, citizens. And in case of army members who happened to suffer during the shelling, no, unless it happened during the time off when they would be home. And I mean shelling now, if they would be here and there, a military conscript, that is, a member of BH, amongst other civilians. But this was usually -- but that was usually done by a different commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And did the shelling investigations that you conducted also follow a similar type of methodology?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Would you receive perhaps a phone call from the hospital and you would start by interviewing or speaking to the victims in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, same methodology.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And then you would make an attempt to ascertain the source of the shelling; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. The method that we used to pass information was always the same; from the hospital, then collection of whatever information, and then going out to the site. And if there were several such places, then we would inform the headquarters so that we could have a team with the investigating judge going out, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And during 1993, if you recall, how frequently was the Dobrinja area shelled?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dobrinja was shelled on a number of occasions in 1993, but again, it varied. At times there would be very frequent bouts of shelling, and yet there would be also periods of time when there was no shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How about 1994, was the situation largely the same with respect to shelling?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, likewise in 1994. There were cases recorded when there were shellings and many casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sokolar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions at this time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Ms. Pilipovic, is the Defence ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Sokolar, you will now be examined by Ms. Pilipovic who is Defence counsel for the accused. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Sokolar.

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us if, between September 2000 and 8th of November, 1995, you gave two statements to OTP investigators?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the first year?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Easy. You gave your first statement on the 8th of November, 1995, and that statement you signed.

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made a statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your second statement is of the 4th of September, 2000, and you signed that statement, too.

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the counsel and the witness please break between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sokolar, yesterday you told us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, we have a technical problem. You are both speaking the same language and that means that you respond immediately to what Ms. Pilipovic asks you, but then the interpreters have some difficulty in following this high-speed conversation, I would say. So would you please look at your screen, wait until it stops moving so then it has all been translated well into the transcript, and please then answer. I'm quite sure that you'll forget about it and I'll remind you then. That's what always happens. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sokolar, you told us that you completed your education, that you came out of the police school, that is, police academy at Vrace; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I graduated from the school in 1983, in June. 1973, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't tell me that was the police school at Vrace. Was it or wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I see it says 1983. 1973, and yes, it is in the locality of Vrace.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, when answering my learned friend's questions, you said that on the 1st of March, 1992, according to you, as a result of the referendum and the murder of a member of a wedding party, of a Serb member of a wedding party at Bascarsija, barricades had been put up in different parts of the city of Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is. The referendum took place on the 1st of March, 1992, and that day, I was in Dobrinja. But in the evening, I learned that that member of the Serb wedding party was killed in Bascarsija, the old part of the town. And at night, I believe that same evening -- well, not barricades but some checkpoints, men with caps on their heads would put -- were posted on the -- at the crossroads, at the intersections, and with automatic weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know who those men were with caps on their heads at these checkpoints as you call them?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not go that way. I did not pass those checkpoints so I had no opportunity to see those men. But at the places they were posted, it was in the vicinity of areas with the Serb major so I presume they were citizens of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, since you have now confirmed to us that it was an assumption on your part that those checkpoints were in the areas where there was a Serb majority and that they were therefore Serb barricades, and what about the parts of the city where the Muslim majority were Serb checkpoints or barricades put up there? I'm sure that you can give us a more precise answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the part of the city where I lived and where I moved around, even though I endeavoured to move as little as possible because of the danger involved, there were also these checkpoints set up with masked persons. I mean they had masks on their heads. I did not walk around these areas. But in the Aleja Bosne Srebrene, near the barracks, at the intersection of the -- Aleja Bosne Srebrene, and the highway from Stup, then as you come out from Dobrinja to Mojmilo. And I never walked in the direction of Rajlovac but I believe there was another checkpoint there near the petrol station towards Rajlovac. I'm telling you I did not move very much around because of the danger involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, were Muslim barricades put up in parts of the city?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so, in some places, but it was only to prohibit the movement of persons on one side and on the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You worked for the law enforcement agency in the city. Can you tell us, how did the police of the city of Sarajevo react? Do you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the 5th of May, until, that is, we all worked together, policemen of Bosniak, Serb, and Croat ethnicity, we received reports from citizens that cars were being seized or some sidearms, small arms, pistols and things like that. But we could not really engage in solving those cases because it was a major hazard, I mean going there and trying to help those citizens.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: If I understand your answer properly, you have just told us that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript, I believe having heard, but I'm not quite sure, the witness mention the 5th of April. Just a moment. And what I read in the transcript is the 5th of May, so could the question please be asked once again in order to have the transcript clarified. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you please tell us until when did the Sarajevo police work together? When I say together, I mean Muslims and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was until the 5th of April, 1992, and in the morning they simply did not show up for work. So the number did come. I apologise. Throughout the war, we had a certain number, albeit a small number of Serb ethnicity, of Croat ethnicity, and also reserve force of Serb and Croat ethnicity. But a relatively small number.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you answer what was the reason for -- why did the police part company along the ethnic lines? Was it preceded by a conflict, by some division at Vrace in the school or something?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not properly informed so I do not really know what happened in the school at Vrace. I know there were some difficulties there. I know that that evening at Krtelj there was a special police unit. There were some -- there was some falling out. I don't know what really happened, but I know that they simply parted company and that everybody seized whatever property there was. That was at Krtelj, near the airport.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You just told us there was a conflict in a special unit. Can I understand that within the police force of the city of Sarajevo, or perhaps at the republic level of the MUP, were there special units?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were special units before the war. There were special purpose units.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether it was also the case during the conflict in Sarajevo? And the time I'm talking about is from April 1992, perhaps March 1992, until, as far as we are concerned, September 1994. Do you know about any activity of special units in the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Because I was in Dobrinja, I know that on the 5th of April, so the special unit fell apart. One part stayed in the city, and the others left.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether a part of the special unit which stayed in the city, do you know under whose control this unit was, whether under the control of MUP or any individuals? Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was under the control of the MUP, and then MUP was, formationally speaking, under the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that MUP was later, formationally speaking, under the BH army, do you think you can tell us in which period this was? And again, I should remind you we're talking from April 1992 until September 1994.

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I cannot tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us if this special unit had any special purpose when we're talking about sniping activity? Was this a sniping unit within the MUP which was active in Sarajevo under the nickname of "Seva"?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on after the war I may have heard about it, but during the war I haven't heard about it during the war. I have heard now in the press, in the media that they are talking about these units. But during the war I had no idea about the existence of such units.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, you told us that in May 1992, your duty post was a police station in Dobrinja from the 10th of May. I think that's what I understood on this; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not from the 10th of May. I think it was the month afterwards, June or July.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you came to this duty post, where was it exactly? And could you tell us how many people were employed in that station?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HQ was in a changed shop, which was a business premises, and this became the offices. And the number varied. There were dozens of people coming, going. There was not a permanent staff there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us about this station. In which street in Dobrinja, this business shop, this business premises as you say, where was it?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in Nehruova Street, in the ground floor building where there was a furniture showroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Considering that we find it easier, if you'd tell us which part of Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Dobrinja II.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So it was Dobrinja II. So was there a hospital in Dobrinja II as well?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a little below -- across the intersection, in the other apartment blocks.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether in that part of Dobrinja there was also a brigade, brigade HQ, the brigade that was in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, just to clarify the transcript, this has to do with Dobrinja II. I believe that was missed in the transcript as pertaining to the answer of the witness. I am talking about line 17 of page 23 where the number is not present, but we did all hear Dobrinja II, including the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that the furniture showroom was in Dobrinja II. Mr. Sokolar, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was in Dobrinja II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, since you told us about the location of the police station where you worked, do you know whether in that part of Dobrinja, there was also HQ of the 5th Motorised Brigade which was in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had units in all areas of the -- on the edge of Dobrinja, but I don't know where their HQ was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The 50 people who worked as policemen for Dobrinja, could you tell us, what kind of equipment they had? You told us that you were a plainclothes policeman, and were there also some of your colleagues who were wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was all a mixture of colours really, of clothes. Also in terms of uniforms, I said that a reserve force of the police had been mobilised, so a number of policemen from November, that is, from the new year, beginning of 1992, there were policemen who had blue uniforms, thicker uniforms. And they wore them for a while, and then some of them came in civilian clothes; some of them wore jeans or whatever they had. Part uniform, part civilian. But it was a very small number really wore a uniform. Mostly wore civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether they had been issued with weapons?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that for a short period of time they had been issued automatic rifles because this was what had been left over from before the war. Formationally speaking, they should have been issued with these kinds of weapons. But later on, they were not carrying these weapons. Perhaps for a short period in 1992 they did wear -- they did carry the weapons, and then they only with went automatic pistols.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say for a short period in 1992, do you think you can tell us exactly which period this was that your colleagues had been issued with rifles?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this was only until about August. I don't think it went on until September 1992. These are just the first two months, just the beginning of the war clashes. And then later on, they wore -- they had weapons because they were patrolling with other organs, and then they just had pistols.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you told us about the police force in Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I remind both of you to wait until the text stops moving. I know it's very difficult but you are both violating the rules a bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you. We will do our best.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us -- rather, yesterday you told us about the reserve police force. Could you give us more details about what kind of unit that was and under whose command they were?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that the number of the people buried (as interpreted), and I believe there were about 50 policemen. We had our superior whose seat centre in Novi Grad, in Promeska Street (phoen) where there had been a police station before the war. I think that -- I don't think, I know that our managing official was Luban Milos, and then later on it was Mr. Krivic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us about the reserve police force, whether this reserve police force had been issued equipment and weapons?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had been issued.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you give us an answer as to how many people made up the reserve police force and what they had been issued in terms of weapons and equipment?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the equipment was concerned, there was no equipment. They wore civilians clothes. And as -- in relation to weapons, I told you already that they had automatic rifles the first two months, and then -- later on they just had pistols.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In that period in 1992, that's what we're talking about, 1992, do you know whether members of the reserve police force had taken part in conflicts, in battles, on the battlefield in combat?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived in Dobrinja in July, and I think there was a front line already established. And whether members of the reserve police force had been on the battlefield, I don't know. They could have been, because we couldn't leave Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, considering the witness's answer to this question, the Defence would like to show the witness one or two lines from his statement that the Defence has both in English and in Serbian. This is a statement from the 4th of September, 2000. The Defence also has the version in English. We have eight copies. I believe that we can also just give it to the interpreters. And the number is 0156539, and the statement is from the 4th of September, 2000. And that is part of the statement that the Defence would like to show to the witness. This has to do with the witness's answer. This is page 4 of the English version, and paragraph 6. The last three lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the usher please bring the documents to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the interpreters' booths so that -- yes, please, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, my case manager has informed me that we already provided these statements to the interpreters. When we call a witness, we provide the statement to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You are assisting. You may even have double copies which is a great joy for me to establish.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you first like to show just the signature of the witness. Because it's our procedure, Madam Registrar, that we do not tender these things usually, just the few lines that are read, but we first check whether this is the statement the witness signed. Would you please, yes, show it to the witness, not read it, but just to identify whether this is the document containing his statement that he signed. Mr. Sokolar, do you recognise your --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- signature on it? Please return it to Ms. Pilipovic. Ms. Pilipovic, please confront the witness with the part you would like to show him. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, in the part of the statement that I will quote to you, and this part is the last paragraph, you say: "There were about 50 or 60 civilian reserves. Initially between April and September 1992, the reserve police were sent to the front lines. I didn't go to the front line because we were short of weapons. About four or five policemen were killed defending Dobrinja." You answered my question when I asked you, you said you did not know. In 2000, in September, you said that the reserve police force, in April to September 1992, had been sent to the front. Do you think you could tell us what is the truth?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you said battlefield, front, I really meant outside of Sarajevo. However, all this happened before I arrived in Dobrinja. The reserve policemen were patrolling the edges of Dobrinja, and in a certain sense they were defending their own homes. In that sense, they were participating in the war. They were defending their homes. If you can call that a battlefield, a front, then it is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I was just reading what you had stated. Thank you. So now we agree that there were about 50 or 60 civilian reserve policemen who were in reserves an who had taken part in May -- in April, in the battles around Dobrinja; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until I arrived, there were already established there, they were probably on the edges. Not probably, they were on the edges of Dobrinja. And that's how the demarcation line had been established. On one side there was one police and on the other side there was the other police, and that's how the demarcation line was established.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So from your answer, I can conclude that in April and in May, considering you said you arrived in June in Dobrinja, that it was in that part in Dobrinja that demarcation lines, confrontation lines, had been established, and that these lines had divided Dobrinja as you just explained it. You said there were police on one side and police on the other side. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not just the police. There were also citizens who later on became part of the BH army. These were citizens. This was a self-organising of people. Perhaps it was only 10, 15 reservists. And then there was a division between Dobrinja IV and Dobrinja III, and Dobrinja I, and then our part of Dobrinja I so to speak, and on the other side of Nedzarici. Yes, the division came to be in this place -- in this way. The police was patrolling in Dobrinja, and this is how the division happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us about the demarcation lines that were established in April, May 1992. In the course of 1992, 1993, until September of 1994, did they change or did they remain as they were established then? Do you have any knowledge of that? Was there combat? Were there clashes?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only a small part behind Dobrinja V. I think that the main lines shifted a little. But this was more army -- against the army. Perhaps between Nedzarici and Dobrinja V. But in other parts, these were apartment blocks. No, no, the lines did not shift. There was no significant shifting of lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the period until 1994, I mean from the moment until you arrived in Dobrinja to the police station, could you tell us whether apart from the police that had weapons, whether other people or perhaps units who were also moving in that part of town and that were also armed? You're a policeman so you're probably quite well informed. I wonder whether you can give us an answer to this.

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Considering that there were few weapons, most of the weapons were probably on the front lines, in these buildings. So inside Dobrinja itself, I never saw people in large groups with weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you didn't see people in large groups, what do you mean by a large group of people?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: A unit, from one part of Dobrinja to another part of Dobrinja. I'm talking I would see two or three people, policemen. Inside -- inside Dobrinja, I did not see large groups of people.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "large groups of people," a large unit, what do you mean? Were there smaller groups of people that were armed and were present in Dobrinja? Have you had reports that these groups may have been mistreating citizens or carrying out burglaries of apartments? Have you heard any such information? I will remind you. Was there a group that was under the control of Juka Prazina, Caco, Dr. Loncarevic? Do you know any such information?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked on crime prevention and I worked on burglaries, I worked on robberies. But in that period, I could only talk to people and investigate and interview people, citizens who were not members of the armed forces. In fact, I spoke with only underage people and women who were not military conscripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us under whose control the reserve police was in the area of Dobrinja in the period from April/May 1992? And I mean the reserve police force that we agreed had taken part in battles. Under whose control were they?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until I arrived, the main person in charge was Mr. Krivic, Malik Krivic. And then people changed, people were transferred. They were transferred for all kinds of reasons. So in these units, smaller units, I don't know, until I arrived. But later on, during the war, after I arrived, I found Mirko Lovric who was of Croatian ethnicity. He was in Dobrinja for about two to three years to follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you tell us about these smaller units that were in neighbourhoods, how many people made up these smaller units, and how come they were based in the neighbourhoods?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this was in the settlement of Buca Potok, in Alipasino Polje, and I can't quite remember. These were smaller units just like in Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any information or knowledge whether -- in what kinds of facilities these units were based in those parts of town? Were these business premises? Were these apartment blocks?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was only in Alipasino Polje that there was a -- that their base was in the ground floor apartment block, but I don't know about this. I was in Dobrinja so I don't really know where exactly they were based. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Today, or perhaps yesterday, to the question of my colleague, you said that the police in Dobrinja, that is, your unit, reported to the Novi Grad station. Did I understand you correctly? You said that that was the security service -- public security centre of Novi Grad; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we had to report to the centre. But it's not the centre of public security; this is the public security station, Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you sent your reports to the public security station in Novi Grad. Do you have any information to whom the Novi Grad public security station reported? Who was then their immediate superior to whom the reports went?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably to a higher instance, it would have been the CSB, Security Services Centre. Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, when you were sending your reports to the Novi Grad station, what did your report consist of, and when did you send that? How many times a day? Was it a daily report, was it a weekly report, or was it a monthly report? And what exactly did it consist of?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like you to tell me, clarify exactly what kind of report you mean. I sent these official reports that you were able to see. I also sent official reports if I identified a perpetrator, and then I would send it to the public security station, and then they would send it on. Official notes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Who did you send the official notes to, and how often?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The official notes, if there was an incident, a wounding incident or a shelling incident, so during the day, on that afternoon, for instance, if I was able to or the following day, if it was technically possible, if there was no electricity or the fax wasn't working, then I would have to do it the following day. I didn't send any weekly reports or any monthly reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you sent official notes and you told us about what they contained. You then sent those to the Novi Grad station. Do you know to whom the Novi Grad station sent these reports or these official notes that you compiled?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am repeating: I would send to my superior, to my station, and I presume that they would then send that to the security services station in the town, to the centre. It's not within my realm of competence to decide to whom it would go. I would do my official note, send it to my centre. And then which part would then go to the CSB or which one would remain there, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can see that it is time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Ms. Pilipovic. We'll adjourn until 11.00. But before we leave this courtroom, I'll just give you a bit of my bookkeeping. I think the examination-in-chief took approximately one hour and 50 minutes. I think you are now 40 minutes so it's -- you are not at your time yet, but just to remind everyone that we are keeping our time limits rather strict. We adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. Usher. Once the witness has been brought in the courtroom, you may proceed with the cross-examination, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, before the break, we were talking about the official notes that you made. You said you submitted a note to the Novi Grad station, and that you assume they forwarded them on but you, I think, said that you didn't know who it was that sent them on. Can you please confirm if I interpreted your words right?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us if you have any -- are you aware that in April, May, or June 1992 a state of war was proclaimed or a state of imminent danger of war in Sarajevo? Do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The referendum for the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina was on the 1st of March. On the 5th or 6th of April, Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised by the United Nations, and I think that sometime in April or -- maybe I'm not quite sure. Yes, that's quite true, the imminent danger of war was proclaimed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: But can you tell us what when, what month?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Was it after the recognition by the United Nations in April? I don't know, I'm not ...

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, in the course of your work in the Dobrinja station, have any knowledge that because that specific body was set up in Dobrinja following the proclamation of the imminent danger of war involving members of the Civil Defence, police reserve forces, so on and so forth, and that body was then put in charge of organising the defence; or to organise because the imminent danger of war was proclaimed? Was anybody set up or did everybody there act separately? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning, people organised themselves, and I don't mean only Dobrinja, with the help of the police. They stayed there in Dobrinja. But I didn't quite get your meaning. What organisation do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether there was a body in charge. Was it within the Civil Defence?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a Civil Defence staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And what about the municipal authorities? Were they operational at the time? Do you have any idea?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the municipality was in a different part of the city -- I mean the Novi Grad municipality, and it was in working order. But what bodies were really operational at that time, I really do not know. As I told you already, we seldom could get from the municipality to other parts of the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you mostly discharged different duties in your locality. Can you tell us, since you were a member of the police and that you were issued with a pistol when on duty, are you a policeman or are you a civilian regardless of what kind of clothes you're wearing?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was issued with a pistol, with just a sidearm, but I carried it very seldom. If I did, I would have it in a special holder. And how did I feel? Well, I felt like a civilian since I was not in a uniform though I worked in the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you did not know exactly where was the headquarters of the BH army in Dobrinja. During your work and movement throughout Dobrinja, would you come across soldiers who were members of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: For two or three years, but those were groups of men in civilian clothes so that you couldn't say really. And towards the end of the war, I would see threesomes or foursomes, uniforms, moving through Dobrinja, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. moving around.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And those groups of armed men that you saw in Dobrinja, what was the relationship between those groups of men and you as a policeman responsible for law enforcement, for law and order and crime suppression? Did you have any communication with them? Did you approve their conduct?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat that I was not responsible for them. Not even the uniform part of the police were in charge of these men. We never conducted any investigation on the front line where army members perished. That was simply outside our terms of reference.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say in that part of Dobrinja, when it comes to the army, there was the military security in place?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I guess so.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, who was the commander of the military security in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if, in 1992, 1993, 1994, there was in Dobrinja a unit commanded by a man nicknamed Dedo, and that that unit was under the BH army's control? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness indicates with his head that he doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You, as a policeman, can you tell us if -- when incidents happened as those sniper incidents or shelling incidents as my learned friend asked you, did you always go out to conduct an on-site investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The interpreters could not hear the answer to your last question, Ms. Pilipovic. Could you please repeat the question or invite the witness to repeat his answer. Perhaps I'll read the question again to you. The question was: "You, as a policeman, can you tell us if -- when incidents happened as those sniper incidents or shelling incidents as my learned friend asked you, did you always go out to conduct an on-site investigation?" That was the question of which we could not hear the answer. Would you always go out?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Situation permitting. That is, I could do on some occasions in case of shelling, depending on the position of buildings and so on and so forth. That is, if it was safe enough, then I would go to the site. If it was a sniper incident, then I would come close to the place, 10, 15 metres, perhaps, away from the site of the incident to see the location, to see the site where a person had been victimised. I wouldn't expose myself to danger by going to the very same place. I would be somewhere in the vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us if -- can you tell us if you keep your own archive for 1992, 1993, 1994 specifically?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean my only personal?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the official notes that you made.

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not keep the official notes. And since I've retired since, I have none of those documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, what was your duty during an investigation on site?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: My duty when investigating on site was to establish the direction in which the victim had been moving, the direction from which the projectile had come, rather, where the person had been injured, to establish the location of buildings and other circumstances. It varied from one case to the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, in 1992, 1993, 1994, whilst engaged in these duties, could you tell us, how many such cases did you have? How many such investigations did you conduct?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, I did not do it, nor in the beginning of 1993. It was only as of mid-1993, I think, that I started conducting these investigations. And the number, I've already said here that there were days when there would be two or three instances, and then four or five days would pass without any investigation. But even during the ceasefires, perhaps a longer time might elapse between two incidents. I can't really remember it all.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I will remind you in your statement of the 4th of September, 2001, on page 4 of the B/C/S version - in the English version, it is page 6 - second passage, and I'll read it out to you. You said that: "During the war, I made well over 200 forensic investigations concerning the shelling and sniping incidents in the area of Dobrinja." Is this accurate, what you said here?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's slightly with the translation here. I was present at about 200 investigations, because I wasn't always there all by myself. But I've already said when there will be more casualties, whether dead or wounded, that I would be a team, an investigating team, and I believe there was quite a number of such instances.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, according to you, as a man engaged in such investigations, what do you understand by "forensic investigation"?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know -- I cannot speak English, but I think that in translation it means some expert analysis. We call it criminal investigation. But this is not -- this was not up to me. All that I did was collect the data about the injured, the location of buildings, of the victim, things like that. And I would assist other members of the team when a team was out. So I did not conduct any criminal forensic investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: But would you agree that forensic investigation means judicial investigation, when there is a forensic pathologist, an investigating judge and all the other experts? Were such investigations conducted during that period of time, in 1992, 1993, 1994? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were such investigations.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Now, you, when you said that you would usually be on your own, or at times with a team, would you draw a sketch of the incident site or take photographs of the scene of the incident?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not make any sketches or photographs because that is part of the job of the criminal investigation assistants. In a certain matter, I would visually inspect the site and then write the official note. But this was done only in case of woundings. And in more serious cases, a whole team would come out. As for the photographs, we didn't have things to photograph with, cameras or anything, at least in Dobrinja. I suppose that at the city level they did have some.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So when drawing up your official notes, you would never measure the distances, that is, from the place from which the shot came from?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I did not make any measurements. I would merely determine the direction on the basis of the victim's posture and location of the buildings. The distances, no, I did not measure them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: From what I can gather about your role, when drawing up the official notes, you were not an eyewitness to these events, were you?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't the eyewitness. When somebody would be injured, I would turn up after the event, either to the scene or after the person had been brought to the hospital. I wasn't an eyewitness to these incidents.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: But prior to you going out to the scene where it was said that an incident had happened, would you have before that an interview with victims in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a certain number of cases, if the persons were in such a state, I would exchange a couple of sentences with the victims in Dobrinja to merely establish the direction of movement. Of course, if the victim was able to speak. If not, then I would talk to the hospital personnel. Or, for instance, if the person had been taken to the city, to the hospital in Kosevo, then I would simply go out to the scene of the incident and collect information.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: From your answer, I understand that information about the scene of the incident and the place or rather the direction from which - how shall I put it - the fire came from, that this information you collected, you obtained from the victim; is that it?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said in a certain number of cases, I would speak to the injured person in the Dobrinja hospital. But with a certain number, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: As a person engaged in these duties, can you confirm to us whether those official notes that you made were drawn up duly, properly, as they should be drawn up? You told us also that you made no sketches, no photographs, took no measurements. Were, then, those official notes credible? Did they reflect properly the scene of the -- the scene which you attended to?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As it is -- it was a larger number of notes, one couldn't draw up the conventional record of the investigation, so this was the brief as possible record, without adding measurements or something. And in various instances where one could not make any measurements because of the danger involved. One goes out to the site and stays there the shortest time possible because there was always a danger from repeated shelling or sniping. So I would go out there, see it, and then put it on paper. Of course, in line with my knowledge, with my experience, with my expertise.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us today that you received a criminal complaint regarding an incident which happened in May, that you were shown an official note, that is, an official note of the 25th of May, 1994. In this official note, you noted that a bus had been hit. Did you see that bus, about which you claim it was at a bus stop in the street of Nikole Demonje Street?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that I did not find that bus there because the bus had left the scene. Whether taken away, the victims or somebody. I told you already it wasn't on the scene. It had gone to the base or to the depot where buses are parked.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And after you received the information about the incident, and you said that a bus had gone to the depot, did you that day or some other day, did you go there to the depot and see the bus, and did you take note of the damage done to the bus, or rather the exact location of the damage?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not go in the days that followed to the depot because it is in a different part of the Novi Grad municipality, but I believe that my colleagues who worked near the depot went there. Whether they drafted a report or something or whether they took any forensic experts, I do not know. I wrote my note, I notified them, and then they took whatever further steps.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: From your official note which you had an opportunity to see, I will read out to you that you said that the bus had been hit in the front right wheel. On the basis of what information, since you told us that you had not seen the bus, on the basis of what did you then submit to us this note and say that it was the right front wheel?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the conversation with my colleagues over the telephone who told me that they had come out and established this. I did not see the bus.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
