utterances.text: [Interpretation] In view of the legal importance which this fact could have with regard to this hearing, I should like to indicate to the Chamber, because this is a very contradictory statement, that this witness has indicated just a moment ago on page 9, line 5, and this is a little bit after the place where the witness -- line 7, to be more precise, where the witness -- I'm referring you to line 7, if you will look at the answer about the tyre, about the damage done to the tyre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you are commenting on the witness statement, which is not what you're supposed to do during cross-examination. Whatever questions may be asked, you may tell your colleague to confront the witness with an earlier part of his testimony in court. But it's not for counsel who is not cross-examining the witness to interfere and comment on what are things to look at specifically by this Chamber concerning this examination. Would you please keep that in mind. Of course, you can cooperate with lead counsel as you wish, but this is not what we actually understand by cross-examining the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Mr. President. It is merely to help the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So, Witness, are you telling us now that in the official note you said that the front wheel had been hit on the basis of the information received from your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. On the basis of the conversation that I had with my colleagues, and on that basis, I wrote my note; in what form I do not know. But I believe it says "wheel," and that the bullet ricochetted. Whether it was in the area of the wheel, I do not know. I'm telling you that I did not inspect the bus because it had left the scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, when did you get this information from your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was the next day.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We cannot hear the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was the next day because --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: One of the microphones is switched off or the witness did not say anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the interpreters have difficulties in hearing you. Perhaps, Mr. Sokolar, if you do not lean too far backwards, then you are closer to the microphone and the interpreters will be better able to hear you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us, on the basis of what -- on the basis of what parameters did you establish, since you told us that you had not taken any measurements, photographs, or sketches, on the basis of what did you establish that the projectile that hit the bus came from the locality of Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after I went to the hospital and gathered the information Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that was already mentioned about the victim and the type of injury, I came out. I went out to the scene where the bus had stopped after entering Dobrinja, and I took note -- I took visual note of the scene, of the location of the buildings, established that a bullet had come from the right, that is, from the direction of Nedzarici, because my colleagues had told me over telephone that the bus had been hit on its right-hand side next to the wheel. Perhaps it wasn't the wheel. Perhaps it was my mistake when I said wheel. It could have been wheel or the area around the wheel.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, how do you explain, then, the fact that the official note was drawn up on the 25th of May and that it said that it was written that day, and now you tell us that the information about the incident as regards the place where the bus was hit you received the next day from your colleagues? Can you explain that? Would you allow that you drew up this official note later?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The official note was written either on that day or the following day, but it has -- it bears the date of that day so that we could have easier administration of these notes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you will allow for the possibility that the official notes of this type, that these notes that you compiled, you and your colleagues as well, that these notes could have been compiled later, after the event or after the incident was reported? So after receiving the information.

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember the exact time of the day. It could have happened that I may have been informed on the same day by the colleagues. Whether the bus may have been hit in the morning, I don't quite remember now. But it could have happened that it was in the afternoon that I was informed, and then I wrote the official note. I cannot quite recall now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Since you had your conversation, I believe that I'm correct that you spoke to the victims -- the victims who were on the bus on the critical day. Do you know at which height were the injuries located on the bodies of the people who were on that bus? Do you have this information?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand. What height do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to their bodies, how high on their bodies were the injuries?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I spoke to the victims, I believe that I came to the conclusion that they had already sat down on the bus and that they were injured in the area of the upper leg. I believe that one victim had one leg injury and the other one had both legs injured, as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you spoke to them, did you establish whether they were sitting or standing at the time?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. There were many cases, and I really cannot remember because of time that has lapsed. I don't have that ability to remember all the dates and all the victims, because many things happened. Really, I cannot answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you perhaps answer the question whether in that period, while you were doing your work, do you know whether from the parts of Dobrinja - and I believe that we have by now established that Dobrinja had been divided into Dobrinja I, II, III, IV, and Dobrinja I and IV were under the control of the Republika Srpska army, and then Dobrinja II, III, and V and part of Dobrinja 1 were under the control of the BH army - do you know whether in these parts of Dobrinja there was firing and sniping activity in the direction of Nedzarici, Dobrinja I and Dobrinja IV? Do you have any information, any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the direction -- from the direction of Dobrinja IV -- I'm sorry, you've just confused me with this question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Whether from Dobrinja I, II, III, and V, I mean part of Dobrinja I, was there firing from weapons or sniping activity, or from mortars, from those parts of Dobrinja in this activity in the direction of Dobrinja IV and parts of Dobrinja I and to Nedzarici? These were parts, as we have agreed, these were parts of town which were under the control of Republika Srpska army. Do you have information or knowledge about the combat or firing from those parts of town towards Nedzarici, Dobrinja IV, and parts of Dobrinja I in 1992, 1993, and 1994?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, there were combat operations, but this was from the edges, on the confrontation line, on the demarcation line, and it was well known in which some apartment blocks there were BH army members and then the Republika Srpska army members. But this was on the edges. Of course there was an exchange of fire but it was on the edges, not inside.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to the demarcation line towards Nedzarici, could you tell us which edge parts were under the control of the BH army in relation to the demarcation line towards Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were buildings Oktobarske Revolucije Street and Danka Mitrova Street. These are buildings on the rim, on the edge. But also towards Nedzarici, there were also houses, smaller houses, maybe one or two floors where Bosniak citizens lived. And further down, there was a demarcation line. So there were no apartment blocks, but it was further, deeper into the settlement.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, what was the distance between -- on the line of the demarcation? What was the distance between the two warring lines?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't know unfortunately because I wasn't there. When it was apartment block, apartment block, then there was a demarcation line. But inside the settlement, I did not really have access because there were combat operations and I cannot really go there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any opportunity after Dayton was signed to go to Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In which part? You mean the one that was under the control of the BH or the -- in both parts? Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what was the state of these buildings?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were destroyed, partial. Some of them were complete or partially destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could we agree that in both parts, that is, in both parts of the city - and I'm talking about this part of town, this part of the city, so the part that was under the control of the BH army as well as the part that was under the control of the Republika Srpska army - that these parts of that part of the city were equally destroyed on both sides?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but where the BH army was, there were more destroyed than on the other side. I mean there was more damage on the side of -- they were more destroyed on the BH army side.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could we conclude from that answer that in that part of town, there was frequent fighting?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, there was fighting.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us today that the church had not been completed, had not been finished. Could you tell us a little more about this? What does this mean? Could you perhaps describe specifically? In 1992, 1993, and 1994, was this church in the process of being built, and at which stage had it arrived?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The church was built, and there was scaffolding around, so that's why I am saying it was still under construction. But it was built. There was just scaffolding. You could see the scaffold from the part of Dobrinja under Bosnian control, we could see the scaffolding. It was construction scaffolding.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you see from which part of Dobrinja, you just said under Bosnian control, you can see this church?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The church can be seen from the part of Dobrinja anywhere where you're crossing from Dobrinja II to Dobrinja III. There are three bridges; one is larger for vehicles, and then there are two for pedestrians. And yes, further down below, I cannot quite remember but I believe that you can see it -- the church -- you can see also from another bridge which wasn't operational. You can see it from there. It was a traffic bridge.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, considering that Dobrinja River flows through Dobrinja, looking towards the church, how many bridges are there in Dobrinja that go across -- how many bridges are there that go across the river, considering that you've lived there for a long time and that you moved around that part of town quite a lot?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it necessary to list all of the bridges in the whole of Dobrinja? There was a large bridge on the confrontation line, and there was also where the buses turned, and then there was a bridge where there was a confrontation line where nobody moved. Then there was another bridge, and this was from the Emile Zola Street on to the square. Then number 3, there was a bridge for the traffic, the buses, when the buses could go, when it was possible. And then there was another pedestrian bridge between Dobrinja II and Dobrinja III. And then the third bridge which wasn't operational, and this was also for vehicles, this was in two directions towards Nedzarici. But in Nedzarici there was a newly-built bridge which was under the control of the Republika Srpska army, and this was further down below. So yes, I've given you all the bridges.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Could you tell us in what way and whether these bridges were protected, as far as you can recall.

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that when these victims had been hit, I can't quite remember, but I don't think they were protected. But I think later on there was some protection. On the large bridge for the traffic, and then ongoing from the street, Emile Zola Street, the larger one was protected as well as the bridge from the hospital towards Dobrinja III. So partially this third bridge closer to Nedzarici was also protected. These were protections that were put up during the war, but when they were exactly put up, I cannot tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you describe for us what kind of protection that was? Specifically, I am asking you about the bridge Emile Zola and also the bridge Dobrinja II and Dobrinja III?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Emile Zola bridge was not protected because it was closer to the confrontation line, and the one further down was protected with large concrete blocks, with large containers. I can't quite remember. There were many different types of protection. In any case, these were concrete slabs. Some of them were even 2 metres by 5 metres, maybe up to 5 metres high. I think later on they were protected. That was the large bridge. But the Emile Zola bridge was not protected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, may I remind you, as I said before the break, that you did not yet use the similar time as the Prosecution did. Now you certainly did. I didn't want to remind you earlier, but could you please give us an indication on how much time you still need?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation Your Honour, I will ask another two questions, and then if you'll allow it, my colleague will also have two questions. We'll be very brief.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you tell us, if you know, how many people were employed at the Security Services Centre in Sarajevo? Do you have that information?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That number varied. I know that in Dobrinja there were about 50 people. How many were there in the centre of the town, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the official notes that you compiled at the time that you went out to the site of incidents were official notes that you drew up according to some of your personal observations?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in some cases. This was just for the purpose of recording all the incidents. It was technically not possible to do it if you paid attention to every single detail. You need an expert, you need a team to put -- as you said yourself, all those technical details, forensic details. This was just to go out to a site, short description, visual distance, position, movement, direction. No, I did not measure distance, not in metres anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you agree with me that a team going to a site, really we should have a ballistic expert present, and if there was shelling, for instance, in question, in order to have some more precise data?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Expert teams would go out on the sites, and a ballistic expert, forensic expert, also technical staff. Yes, professionally that's how it would have to be done.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: One more question, please. As far as you can recall after the incident that happened in Dobrinja on the 4th of February, 1994, when the shelling happened of the queue for water, as far as you can recall, from that date, was there shelling in Dobrinja in 1994? Do you remember, or there weren't any?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 4th of February, I was -- I was wounded, and it wasn't a water queue, but I believe that in those premises, humanitarian help was being administered opposite to where I was working. It was in the other part of Dobrinja, and there were three or four shells that landed. I was wounded. And after that 4th of February, yes, there was shelling. In 1994?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was shelling afterwards. What kind of shelling do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Specifically in Dobrinja where you lived.

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Even after that February 1994, there was shelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, according to your memory, some locations?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: 15th of July, in C5 block, in 1993. The 1st of June, Dobrinja III. I really cannot remember. After that date, some more significant incidents where there were many victims. If investigations were conducted, probably colleagues went to do these on-site investigations. I cannot quite remember after that date. Then there was a long period that came up to -- running up to Dayton. And I really cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness, and thank you, Your Honour, for the time that I took up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pilipovic. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you have additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the Chamber will authorise me, yes, I will ask very brief questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you have a few brief questions, that's fine. If you could do it just as efficiently as Ms. Pilipovic did, the Chamber would be very happy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try and do even better if that is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, hello, and thank you for being here. You established in one of your statements, your written statements, that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you knew that the Bosnian Army had their HQ in Dobrinja; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. On the other hand, you said that you did not know where the HQ in Dobrinja was; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that this was by units, by companies in Dobrinja I, II, in C5, the airport settlement. There were smaller units, smaller groups. I never saw that -- there was no barracks, there was no place where they all came to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, I understand that there were detachments in each one of all the Dobrinjas that we know about; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, companies, smaller units.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. You just told me that there were no barracks, and I think I understood you correctly there were no barracks in any of the four or five Dobrinjas that we know about; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether they had anything near the confrontation line, the demarcation line, I don't know whether they had barracks there, whether they had, I don't know. But within, inside Dobrinja itself, in the interior, no, they didn't. But what people did is when they would finish their shift, they would go back to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. So where did these soldiers sleep? Where did they sleep?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would go back to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: After they would finish their shift, as far as they stayed on their shift, they would then go home.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. Witness, you spoke about the hospital. In Dobrinja in order to be able to locate exactly where this hospital was, could you please remind us where the hospital was?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hospital was in the -- on the ground floor of the building of Omladinskih Radnih Brigada Street -- on the corner there was a restaurant, and I believe there was also some medical equipment there, and it was on the ground floor of a building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Now that we have the street, do you know which number, street number, that was of that building?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where the numbers start, but this was on the corner of the street, Omladinskih Radnih Brigada. It was the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. That's very well. Now, in that hospital, in the infirmary, was there any kind of sign to denote that this was a hospital?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that there was a sign -- there was no -- anything written, but I cannot remember whether there was a Red Cross or any other sign like that. I knew it was a hospital. I went past there every day but I never really noticed it. Not that it would be visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you said that you went to visit the victims on site, and did you with your own eyes see a sign that was visible so that that would denote a hospital; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Inside Dobrinja, if you would come close to the building, then you would see it. But whether you could see it from a distance, whether there was a sign that you could see from a distance that this was a hospital, this was a ground floor building, I really don't know. I'm not sure about the sign. I cannot tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes, I understand your answer. Thank you. Now, do you know whether there was a prison near the hospital or anywhere near it? I can see that you're smiling.

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I smiled because I was a policeman. I did not have a possibility to keep these people that I would want to keep in custody. I worked with underage people. I didn't have any premises to put them in. I did not have a place to keep them. So there was no prison by the police administration. But whether the military security had any place to keep prisoners of war, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When you say -- so when you say perhaps, does it mean that -- could you be perhaps more precise? You don't know, or is this the latest remark about the military facilities?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you I did not have any access, I did not have authority for a period. Because of certain problems, we were not really in a very good relationship with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you know anything about a cafe called Borsalino or Sunce? Do these names tell you something?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Borsalino is in the area of the municipality of Novi Grad and is located in Alipasino Polje. And Sunce, I don't know. There was a shop called Sunce. But a coffee bar Sunce, no, I don't know that. But Borsalino is on the Alipasino Polje, on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: This cafe, was that a place of detention?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They had a possibility if they needed to keep people, they could have kept it at their centre. They probably had a custody room to keep these people. But whether they had, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution objects to this line of questioning on the grounds of relevance. And I also note again the time issue is ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, could you please respond to the objection of the Prosecution about the relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Because we are trying to establish what were the military facilities in terms of troops, whether they were in civilian clothes or in uniforms, and it seems to me that there were such centres in Dobrinja. And I think that it is legitimate for us to ask whether these various legitimate targets were. And this is what -- this is this line of questioning, whether in this part of Dobrinja, I believe we have to ask this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you the following question: Would you consider prisons as being legitimate targets? I mean, you have been asking a lot about prisons recently.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. No. I will answer differently. I think this is a legal question that I could perhaps return to later. But whoever says prisons has guards, has uniforms, armed people so that's what -- this is where my question was coming from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. Your argument is that if there's a prison, that there are uniformed guards, and that would be a legitimate target then; do I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we have military guards, which is what I think I could understand, if they are standing on duty, service, I believe they are legitimate targets absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't hear anything about standing on duty. So it's your position that -- I do understand that it's part of the case of the Defence which might make that question perhaps relevant that if uniformed, even militarily uniformed people are guarding prisons, that these are legitimate targets; do I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. President, yes, in the sense that if there was a military facility, there are guards normally in uniform. And if there is a conflict, it is natural that the adversary, the opponent will not know what they are doing, these guards. But the opponent will know that these guards are standing to guard something, so that will be a legitimate target, yes, which is where the line of questioning comes from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand you, your position. You indicated, Mr. Piletta-Zanin -- I'll not stop you on this questioning although it might be a complex legal issue. I'll not stop you on that, but I remind you that you said you had only two or three questions, and I know for certain that you can count even to more than ten so you know where you are with the number of questions you've put to the witness. I'll give you the opportunity to finish briefly, and try again to be as efficient as Ms. Pilipovic was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. But life is full of surprises. We know that. We all discover things all the time. But we shall finish here. We do not have any further questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Is there any need to re-examine the witness, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Very briefly on one point, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Sokolar, in your response to a question from my learned colleague, you indicated that, based on what you had said in your witness statement, that you and your colleagues had conducted at least 200 investigations into shelling and sniping; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, in the autumn -- or rather summer of 1992, when the combat operations started, it was only in the latter half of 1993 that these notes and investigations started. I said 200 but I could hardly count. There were days when there would be no such incidents; there were other days when there would be a number of them. But at any rate, the number was quite large.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Sokolar, did you and your colleagues investigate every sniping and shelling incident that occurred in Dobrinja between the middle of 1993 when this process started and continuing through 1994?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe almost all of them, as of mid-1993, until the ceasefire was signed. I mean my colleagues and I. If it wasn't me, then it was some other colleagues of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were there sniping and shelling incidents that occurred before you started investigating them in the middle of 1993?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sokolar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Judge Nieto-Navia has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I'm going to read what you answered referring to the bus incident. Page 9, line 5. You said: "I first went to the hospital where I spoke to the personnel, and I found out about their injuries. The bus, the bus had gone, gone to the garage, and there it is. My colleagues went to the garage and looked at the bus." Could you confirm that? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: My colleagues were notified of the incident; and if they did go out to the scene, they told me by telephone that they had inspected the bus and it had been hit somewhere in the area of the wheel. Whether they performed everything else, whether they had the forensic report from the on-site investigation, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've also a few questions for you. During the cross-examination, you were asked whether you knew anything about sniping, sniping units, within the Bosnia-Herzegovina part of the city or armed forces. You said: "I did not know about that during the war." But you might have heard anything about it after the war. Could you tell us what you heard after the war about such sniping or sniper units? And perhaps first, to start with from whom you heard anything about it and what you heard about it.

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall saying now that there were snipers who acted on the BH army side. But there was the exchange of fire along the confrontation line, the demarcation line by the snipers on both sides. Their names, their identity was not revealed. And even if there were any snipers on the BH army side, well, it must be recorded somewhere. That is how we took note of their side; that is, they also had sniping victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll just try to find the exact location of your testimony. I'm having difficulties in finding it. I apologise for that. I'll see whether I can find it later and first put the next question to you. You told us about the weapons you had as police officers, and you said that in the beginning of the conflict - I would say the first few months - you would also have rifles. But then at a certain moment, you did not need to have rifles any more. You had just pistols because you were patrolling with other organs. Could you tell us which other organs you were patrolling with?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. What organs? What organs do you have in mind? There were other weapons in the police station. That's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me take you back to your testimony in this respect. You were asked: "Can you tell us exactly which period this was that your colleagues had been issued with rifles?" That was the question. And then I read as your answer: "I believe that this was only until about August. I don't think it went on until September 1992. These are just the first two months, just the beginning of the war clashes, and then later on they wore -- they had weapons because they were patrolling with other organs, and then they just had pistols." So you are referring to any combined patrolling which caused you to have only pistols and no rifles any more. Could you tell us what kind of combined patrolling this was, with whom? I was just reading your statement -- your testimony from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps it is an error in translation. There was no patrolling with any other organs. A patrol would be two men or maybe three. But for the first two months, they had automatic weapons. And after that, they only had small sidearms pistols. And I was issued with only a pistol. And at times I carried it with me; at times, I didn't, in its place where it belongs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'll have to check whether this is properly translated or not. It's good that you say that you're not aware of having spoken about combined patrolling with other organs. I cannot check it on the spot right now since I have not got available your original language at this very moment. One of the questions put to you was about any units or groups controlled by Juka Prazina. The question was whether you investigated ever activities of this group. And you answered that your investigations were limited to the extent that they would never cover any members of the armed forces. Would you regard groups under the control of Juka Prazina as Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. members of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the early days, those were self-organised groups in all parts of the city. And later on, after a major effort was invested, they were placed under the BH army's control. But a lot of time was needed to regulate it all and put it under control. In the early days it was self-organised groups and it was very difficult to conduct any investigations or do anything. And I've already said that our jurisdiction did not extend over the members -- over persons who were members of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. I've got -- I'm expecting Mr. Piletta-Zanin to help me as well. I've got now the place exactly where you answered the questions about sniping and sniping units. I'll read for you the relevant lines, but I'm afraid that I'm -- one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm reading now to you -- it's the other way. It's page 22, line 17. A question was put to you: "Could you tell us if the special unit had any special purpose when we are talking about sniping activity? Was this a sniping unit within the MUP which was active in Sarajevo under the nickname of Seve?" Your answer was: "Later on, after the war, I may have heard about it. But during the war I haven't heard about it during the war. I've heard now in the press, in the media, that they are talking about these units. But during the war, I had no idea about the existence of such units." Perhaps I may put my question more precise to you: Was there any source outside the media from which you heard about this unit or these units with the nickname Seve?

utterances.speaker: REFIK SOKOLAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Emphatically no. During the war, I knew nothing about that. Later on in the press, there was some scandal related to that group, and that is how I learned about this group called Seve or Larks. And they were members of some special unit. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that you are answering --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is nodding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness is nodding and he's nodding in the affirming way. These were my questions to you. This means that we are now at the end of your testimony in this Court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming the long way from Sarajevo to The Hague in order to answer to all the questions put to you by both the parties and by the Bench. You'll understand that it's very important for this Court to have the information available which is brought into this courtroom by the witnesses answering the questions of the parties and the Bench. It is important for this Court in order to reach their decisions. So therefore, once again I thank you very much, and I wish you a safe journey home again. The witness may be led out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Registrar, could you please assist us in the decisions we have to take on the admission into evidence. I think no videos, no 360-degree photographs. I think we have Prosecution Exhibit P3097, but I don't know whether that's the first one or the reports are the first ones. Yes, please. The first one were the reports or the map? I don't remember, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. President, the report was the first one. P2637.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I think attached to it, P2637.1, the English translation for that same document. It's then admitted into evidence. Then we have the map, the marked -- the map with coloured markings on it. That's P3097. That's also admitted into evidence, and I think that there are no other documents tendered. Mr. Mundis, your next witness will be?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ramiz Grabovica, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher, could you please bring in the...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Nieto-Navia pointed out to me that we are seven minutes from the break, so we wonder whether it would be wise to start. But perhaps then I'll explain to the witness. Mr. Grabovica, my attention -- do you understand me? You hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My attention just was drawn to the fact that we are very close to a break we usually have at this time. And since it might not be very good just to start and break off after three, four, or five minutes, I suggest that we'll first have the break, and then after the break we'll start your examination. This would mean that we stop now, so you can take off your headphones again. We'll resume at I would say then quarter to 1.00. --- Break taken at 12.21 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber apologises for resuming late. One of the Judges was kept busy with some other important thing. Mr. Usher, could you please bring in the next witness. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just a few moments. In relation to the time that the Defence took for cross-examination, we apologise for it. We were looking at the clock, but we saw that according to the transcript, the Prosecution took 1 hour 50, according to what you said. So I believe that we took one and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you looked at the clock. And if you've looked precisely at the transcript, you would have seen that it says in the transcript 1 hour 50, and it still has to be checked. So those who prepare the transcript were aware I might have said, which I did in fact, one hour 15. And I don't think that there's any reason at this moment to comment on a totally wrong basis. Thank you. Please, bring in the witness. Mr. Grabovica, you can hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give your testimony in this courtroom, the rules require you to make a solemn declaration. The text of this declaration will now be given to you by the usher, and I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated, Mr. Grabovica. The order in this court is that since you have been called by the Prosecution, you'll first be examined by counsel for the Prosecution, then by counsel for the Defence. And if there's any need, the Judges will put additional questions to you. Mr. Mundis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Grabovica, can you please state your full name and spell your last name, please.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: Ramiz, R-A-M-I-Z, Grabovica, G-R-A-B-O-V-I-C-A.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Could you please state your date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: I was born in 1959.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Grabovica, at the time when the war in Bosnia started, were you living in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were you working at that time?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Who was your employer and what were your job responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: I was a driver in the public transport company. My company consisted of tram transport, bus, minibus transport, and public transportation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what type of --

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: And cable car transport.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What type of vehicles did you drive for the public transportation company?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: At that time, I drove a trolley bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you continue driving a trolley bus once the war started?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: While there was electricity and the network worked, I drove a trolley bus

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did the electricity work for most of the period of the war, or did it not work for most of the period of the war?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: For the trolley buses, the electricity, I'm not quite sure. But there was no more electricity about 15th of April. Until then, I worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know when the electrical system for the trolley bus was restored?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: The network of the trolley buses was established by the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour., Perhaps my colleague's question should be more specific. We're talking about the 15th of April. I did not understand what year that was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see that it has been specified already. Thank you. Please proceed. And thank you, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know the approximate month and year that the trolley buses started running again in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: By the time when the war had ended, it was beginning early 1996, the network was working again. And even today, there are some parts of the network that are not operational.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When the trolley bus network was not operational, did you continue to be employed by the public transportation company?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What did you do when you were unable to drive a trolley bus?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: I was waiting for instructions; and if there was nothing to do, then I would go back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you also drive a diesel-powered bus intermittently during that period?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: At that time, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did there come a time during the course of the war when you drove a diesel-powered bus for the public transportation company?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: In 1994, I started to drive a bus of the public transportation company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And that was a diesel-powered bus. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Shortly after the war began in Sarajevo, did you become aware of sniping incidents?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And in fact, during 1994, was the bus that you were driving for the public transportation company fired upon by a sniper?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: Yes. They could see it from many different directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What month or day in 1994 was the bus that you were driving fired at?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: Once I said it was the 17th of May, but I think my recollection was wrong. And what I believe now, that this was 25th of May. I'm certain of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you remember going to work on that morning?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: I remember well. There was no shooting. It was sunny, and it was bright. I went to work on foot, or I cycled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did the public transportation company operate its vehicles on days when there were no ceasefires?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: It didn't work, and there were buses for Bosniljak (phoen) and for the hospital workers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The public transportation system only functioned when there was a cease-fire. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what were your assigned duties on May 25th, 1994? What were you supposed to be doing for the public transportation company?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: We worked in two shifts, one shift began at 8.00 a.m., and then ended at 12.00. And then there was 12.00 to 5.00 p.m. This was not full time. I worked the first shift. I drove workers from the public transportation company to the Velikih Drveta Street to Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where was the public transportation company located in the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: It was in Alipasino Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Would it be accurate to state that you were driving on a regularly scheduled bus route between Alipasino Polje and Dobrinja on that day?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: Yes. I drove, but it's not Alipasino Polje. It was Alipasin Bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You were driving a regularly scheduled bus route between those two locations on that day?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Approximately how far is the distance between those two points?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: About 10 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And would your job responsibilities on that day have entailed more than one round trip between those two points?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: The bus went every 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How long did it take to drive the bus between those two points?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: Since there was a large number of passengers, it was sometimes 12, 15 minutes even.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And then once you arrived in Dobrinja, you would then turn the bus around and go back into the centre of the city. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: Yes. I would turn the bus after I would collect the passengers, and I would go back to the starting stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall what the weather was like on the 25th of May, 1994?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: Yes. I remember the weather was sunny, and it was bright. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall what time it was when your bus was fired upon?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: I remember it was at 11.40.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And in what part of the city of Sarajevo was the bus at the time it was shot?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: The bus that I was driving, it was at that time in the centre of Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of the street or streets that the bus was on at the time it was shot?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: At the intersection where I had stopped used to bear the name Aleja of some kind. I don't remember the title. But arriving to that spot was on one side was Nikole Demonje Street and on the other side was Omladinskih Brigada Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At the time the bus was fired upon, was it moving or was it stopped?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: The bus had stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were you stopped at an intersection or were you stopped at a regularly scheduled bus stop or was it the end of the bus route? Can you tell us why the bus was stopped?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: This was my last stop as well as the first stop at the intersection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were you waiting to collect the passengers to return to the centre of the city. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How many doors did the bus have for passengers to either exit or enter the bus?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: There were three doors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And as the bus was at this starting point for its trip, were the doors open or shut?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: The doors, all three of them, were open.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was the motor of the bus running at the time?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: The engine was not running.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Why had you turned the engine off?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: Because of a shortage of fuel, we had -- we received very small quantities, and that's why we had to switch the engine off when it was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please describe for the Trial Chamber what you heard and saw at the time the bus was shot.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: I was sitting at my place, driver's place. The door was open. It was quiet. I heard a shot coming from the direction of Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you then hear any noise or commotion coming from the passengers on the bus?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: After the shot, I immediately heard screaming, panic, calling for help.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you then look to see where this noise or panic was coming from?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: I turned around, and there was panic on the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you see if anyone on the bus was injured?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: I saw a woman on the right-hand side was holding on to her knee.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What did you do at that point?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: And on the left-hand side, I saw a woman who was trying to help as well as looking for help. She was all covered in blood.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So you saw two women who were injured on the bus. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where were these two women in relation to one another when you saw them on the bus?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: They were opposite each other, because the bus has seats in two lines. They were opposite each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What did you then do after you realised that two passengers on your bus were injured?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: I wasn't paying attention to the woman whose holding on to her knee but the woman who was bleeding profusely. She had been hit in an artery, and there was a lot of blood. At that moment, I was also in panic, but I realised that I had to drive them to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What did you do at that moment?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: At that moment, I switched on the engine, closed the doors, even though all the other passengers were saying, "Open, open, because the sniper is shooting."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you let any of the passengers off the bus at that moment?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: No, I did not. I closed the doors, started, and because the hospital was about a hundred metres away, I went over the sidewalk and through a grassy patch, and I made it to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Grabovica, do you know the identity of these two women that were shot on your bus that day?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: I did not know any of those passengers on the bus, and that includes those two women.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you ever see those two women again after that day?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you see any passengers wearing military uniforms on 25 May, 1994, at 11.40 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: No, I did not see anyone because all the passengers on the bus were women.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know the approximate age of the two women who were the victims of this sniping?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: I wouldn't know exactly, but I would say middle-aged, 40, 45. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were both the women approximately the same age?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: I don't really remember if they were peers or if one of them was older. I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know if any of the passengers on the bus were carrying any kind of military weapons?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: No, nobody had military weapons, army weapons, in the bus. I repeat that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At the time your bus was shot, Mr. Grabovica, were you wearing a military uniform?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were you carrying any kind of military weapon?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall whether outside of the bus, in the immediate vicinity of where the bus was parked at the time of the shooting, do you recall seeing any military equipment or large military weapons?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: Along the route that I took, I never saw any troops or military equipment except that the military police were somewhere nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how nearby the military police officer was?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't know exactly the structure that housed them. I only know that the military police was somewhere there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At the time the bus was hit, did you see the military police?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: No. It wasn't the military police; it was the local civilian police that exists in every place everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd ask that the witness be shown the videotape which has been marked P328M.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: "THE INVESTIGATOR: Will you please show me by standing at the location where the front of the bus was located at the time it was hit by a bullet to the best of your recollection. "I'll now mark this line with yellow paint. "Could you please show me where the side of the bus was. "I will now mark that line with yellow point. "Could you please show me by standing on the location where to the best of your recollection you were located at the time the bus was hit by a bullet. "I will now mark that with a figure X and a number 1. "Could you please show me by standing on the spot where to the best of your recollection the bullet hit the side of the bus. "I will now mark this spot with an X and a number 2. "To the best of your recollection, can you show me where Passenger A was seated. "THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] Here. "THE INVESTIGATOR: "I will also place a number 3 inside this location. "Could you please show me to the best of your recollection where Passenger B was located. "Mark this spot with an X and a number 4. "Could you please indicate by pointing in which direction the bus was facing. "Could you please indicate by pointing from which direction, to the best of your recollection, you heard the gunshot at or near the time that the bus was impacted by the bullet. "And finally, could you please show me where the back of the bus was located, to the best of your recollection. "I'll mark this with a line."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Grabovica, did you recognise yourself in that videotape?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you comply with the requests of the investigator to the best of your ability, truthfully?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: All that I could remember, I said it then, and I will say it today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd ask that the witness now be shown the 360 degree panorama photo, P3279M.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Grabovica, do you recognise the image that's on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What does that image depict?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: It's up Dobrinja. It is this way that the bullet came from, from the direction of Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Will you please pan the photograph to the right. Stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Grabovica, is this the direction that the bus had come from prior to arriving in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Continue panning, please, to the right. Pause there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Grabovica, is this the direction the bus was pointed in at the time it was fired upon?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. This is the route to the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. If we can just continue panning back to the right to the original view, please. Thank you. I'd ask that the witness now be shown three photographs which have been marked as P3274. You can place the photo that has been marked as "A" in the upper right hand corner on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Grabovica, do you recall meeting with an investigator from the Tribunal previously and being shown this photograph?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: There's a building in the lower half of the photograph that is circled and has hash marks through it or lines through it. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you make those markings on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Why did you mark this building?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: Because this building did not exist at the time when I drove there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What was located at this spot where the building now stands on 25 May, 1994?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly. Those two buildings were under construction or, rather, the foundations had been laid. But they did not exist there. I don't remember what was there. I know that these buildings were not completed. They didn't look as they do now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Would you please place the photograph with the letter "B" on the upper left hand corner before the witness on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Grabovica, does this view represent the direction from which the bullet came which struck your bus?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you place the arrow in the centre at the lower half of this photograph?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: I drew -- I drew it. Whether it's quite accurate, but it is the Nedzarici direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd ask that the third photograph which has been marked with the letter "C" be placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Does photograph C appear to be taken from the same location as photograph B, but with a telephoto lens? Mr. Grabovica? Sir, did you hear the question?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Does the photograph marked C seem to be taken from the same location as photograph B but with a telephoto lens?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: There are some markings with a black marker and a red marker in the centre of this photograph. Did you, in fact, make those markings?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what do those markings indicate? What does the black circle indicate?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: That is where anti-sniper barricades were, kind of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the -- what does the red line and the red hash marks indicate?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: The red one, the red line, is showing the anti-sniper barricades. Those two smaller objects were not there then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Which objects are you referring to in this photograph that weren't there then?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: Those private houses, or perhaps they were there but they were very small.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The -- are you referring, sir, to the two houses that are inside the black circle in the centre of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Grabovica, do you recall how many gunshots you heard at the time your bus was struck?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: At that time, I heard one shot only.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions at this time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Mr. Grabovica, as I indicated to you, you'll now be examined by counsel for the Defence. Will it be Ms. Pilipovic? Yes. Are you ready, Ms. Pilipovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Before I start asking you questions, I'd like to ask you if you gave any statements to the OTP investigators?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when that was? What year, what period of time?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember exactly. Was it 2001? I think that was the year, but what month, I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And if I tell you that it was on the 18th of September, and then on the 26th of September, 2001, will you then confirm it, that that is when it was?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Will you confirm that what you stated in that statement and confirmed with your signature, that that is true?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us that 1994, the month of May, can you confirm, if when you gave the statement to the investigators, you said when the incident had happened?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: I said -- where it says the 17th, I said I was not quite sure of the date, whether it was the 17th or the 25th. But it seems to me that it was the 25th of May rather.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And when is it that you recalled that it was the 25th of May?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: Well, it was after that statement. It came back to me, and then I told them I'm not quite sure about the date. I'm quite sure that it was the latter half of May 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, to resolve this matter of date, there are the statements of the witness. I'd like to ask the witness first if he knows what day it was.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: I don't. Not exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if it was a working day or a holiday?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: A working day.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: A working day. And if I remember, you said that you drove workers.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: Yes, I also drove workers.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you drive workers that day?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: No. That day, my assignment was to drive civilians only.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I will remind you that you gave your statement on the 18th of September, 2001.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if you said then on what day did that happen?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I said the 17th. That is when I said that it was the 17th. But be that as it may, I said I was not positive about the date. I couldn't say whether it was the 17th or the 25th.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And after that statement that you gave on the 18th of September, did the investigators, when you gave your other statement on the 26th, did they ask you again when that incident had taken place? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: I do, and I repeat it again that I wasn't sure about the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you repeat the date which you gave in the statement that you made on the 18th of September, or did you say you did not know?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: Yes, they said --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, tell us, what do you recollect?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, the Defence at this moment does not have the statement in English. I'm referring to the statement of the 26th of September. So I do not know exactly the number of the document. What I do have is the B/C/S version of that. And if my colleagues are agreeable, then from page 2 of the document, I'd like to show the witness a part of his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please read it, and does the interpreters' booth have a copy in the original language?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, we do not.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have only one copy, Your Honour. But I have the document in English, which can help. Not of the 26th. We have the statement of the 18th of September. The statement of the 26th of September, I do not have it in English, and the interpreters do not have it. It's very short. It's only two lines. I can read it, but all we want to ask the witness is to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are expected to prepare copies if you're going to use the statement and if it's not available to the interpreters. And perhaps it might have mislead you this morning that the interpreters had copies. So would you please read it very slowly so that the interpreters can translate it? So you're reading now from the statement of the 26th of September.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I am reading the penultimate passage from the statement: "I did not know Dobrinja well so I do not know where the military facilities were. I do not remember the exact date of the incident except that it happened in May 1994. I may have, in my second statement, mentioned the specific date, but I'm not quite certain about it." Witness, is that true, what you said? Is this your accurate statement?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you then answer on the basis of what did you remember today that it was the 25th of May?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: Because I was asked about the bus plates, and I said that we had pre-war plates on the bus. And in my company, they said that it happened on the 25th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what colour was the bus?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: The bus was red and white.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- you said that the incident happened at 11.30 or 11.40.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: Well, thereabouts. It could have been about half past eleven or 20 to 12. It was before noon, in any event.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And that day, before that time, did you drive that bus along that route, and for how long, or was it your first round?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: No, it could have been my tenth trip. I think it was my tenth trip. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You mean that day?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when and how often did you cover that line in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: I have been with the public transport since 1994, and I first drove a bus.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. You told us that. But I'm asking you before this critical event, how many days or how many weeks before that were you assigned to that particular itinerary?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: Well, it could have been some ten days earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Today when you answered my learned friend's questions, you said that on the 15th of April, 1992, the trolley buses had gone out of use in Sarajevo. Can you tell us why was that, and why didn't the trolley bus work? Was it because of the power shortage?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: That's right. There was no power. There was no electricity to power them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us if some other means of transportation which are power driven, which are electricity driven, are still operational in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: I do not know exactly about the tramways, but I know that the trolley buses went stopped working and the buses went on working.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You say you don't remember about trams. Do you mean that the trams did not work at all, or that perhaps they did but you don't know when?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: The trams did work then.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do I understand you then to mean that that year, 1994, in May, the trams worked?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: In 1994, the trams work up to Cengic Vila or down to the garage. That was the terminal, and that is where it turned on its way back.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say the garage, can you tell us in what part of the city was the garage?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: It is Alipasin Most. That was the depot. The Velikih Drveta.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So are you telling us that the tram operated between the garage, which is near the Alipasino bridge, to Cengic Vila; is that it?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: No. Bascasija to Cengic Vila, and at times it would go on to the garage, that is, to Velikih Drveta, to Alipasino bridge.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you answer, that day when allegedly this incident happened, can you tell us how many passengers were riding your bus at the moment when you were at the terminal?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ GRABOVICA
utterances.text: Well, I said that already. There were about 15 passengers.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my colleague tells me that now is the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you proceed, Ms. Pilipovic, let me just ask the Registry. Since we started ten minutes later, I'd like to continue for another ten minutes, unless of course this courtroom has to be prepared for an afternoon session. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there is an afternoon session in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So unfortunately we are not in a position to continue any longer at this moment, Ms. Pilipovic. I don't know whether this was a suitable moment or not. I interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then adjourn until tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: be reconvened on Thursday, the 14th day of February, 2002, at 9.00 a.m.
